walkthroughs.body_html:
Algorithms — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Algorithms brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Algorithms.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A* differs from Dijkstra's algorithm because A*:
options: Only works on unweighted graphs
Ignores edge weights entirely
Adds a heuristic estimate of the distance remaining to the goal
Guarantees to visit every vertex in the graph

mcqs.q: The worst-case time complexity of linear search on a list of n items is:
options: O(log n)
O(n)

mcqs.q: Does Big-O notation tell you how many seconds an algorithm will take?
options: No - Big-O describes the growth rate of work relative to input size, ignoring constants and hardware; actual seconds depend on the machine and implementation.
Yes - O(n) means the algorithm takes n seconds to run.
Yes - Big-O is measured with a stopwatch.
Yes - heuristics only change the colour of the path found.

mcqs.q: Is quicksort always faster than merge sort?
options: Yes - the name quicksort means it is the fastest sort in all cases.
Yes - merge sort is only used when quicksort is unavailable.
Yes - heuristics only change the colour of the path found.
No - quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n^2) with poor pivots, while merge sort guarantees O(n log n) in every case.

mcqs.q: Can A* use any heuristic and still guarantee the shortest path?
options: Yes - any heuristic works because A* checks every route anyway.
Yes - merge sort is only used when quicksort is unavailable.
Yes - heuristics only change the colour of the path found.
No - the heuristic must be admissible, never overestimating the true remaining cost; an overestimating heuristic can make A* return a suboptimal path.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Time complexity”?
options: A shortest-path algorithm for weighted graphs with non-negative edges, repeatedly settling the unvisited vertex with the smallest known distance.
A measure, expressed in Big-O notation, of how the running time of an algorithm grows as the size of its input increases.
A simple sort that repeatedly steps through the list, swapping adjacent items that are out of order, with worst-case O(n^2) time.
A divide-and-conquer sort that partitions items around a pivot and recursively sorts the partitions; average O(n log n), worst case O(n^2).
